questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in children is:
questions.concept: Minimal change disease accounts for about 80% of childhood nephrotic syndrome, shows normal light microscopy with podocyte foot process effacement on electron microscopy, and responds well to corticosteroids.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults worldwide is:
questions.concept: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is the commonest primary cause of adult nephrotic syndrome, though diabetic nephropathy is the commonest cause overall when secondary causes are included.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A child develops cola-coloured urine, periorbital oedema and hypertension two weeks after a sore throat. Complement studies would show:
options: Low C3 with normal or slightly low C4
questions.concept: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis activates the alternative complement pathway, lowering C3 while C4 remains largely normal; C3 recovers within 6 to 8 weeks. Persistently low C3 beyond that suggests membranoproliferative disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody with linear IgG deposition on immunofluorescence and pulmonary haemorrhage defines:
questions.concept: Anti-GBM disease produces a smooth linear ribbon of IgG along the basement membrane, in contrast to the granular pattern of immune complex disease and the pauci-immune pattern of ANCA vasculitis. Treatment is plasmapheresis with cyclophosphamide and steroids.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The commonest primary glomerulonephritis worldwide is:
questions.concept: IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is the commonest primary glomerulonephritis, classically presenting with synpharyngitic macroscopic haematuria within days of an upper respiratory infection, with mesangial IgA deposits.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes nephritic from nephrotic syndrome?
options: Red cell casts with hypertension and oliguria
questions.concept: Nephritic syndrome is defined by an active urinary sediment - dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts - with hypertension, oliguria and modest proteinuria. Heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia define nephrotic syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The most important complication predisposing nephrotic patients to infection is loss of:
questions.concept: Urinary loss of IgG and complement components, particularly factor B, impairs opsonisation and predisposes to encapsulated organisms, notably pneumococcal peritonitis in children.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with membranous nephropathy is most likely to have autoantibodies against:
questions.concept: Autoantibodies against the M-type phospholipase A2 receptor on podocytes are found in about 70 to 80% of primary membranous nephropathy and are useful for diagnosis and monitoring. Subepithelial deposits give a spike-and-dome appearance.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Nephrotic syndrome carries a high risk of thrombosis chiefly because of:
options: Loss of antithrombin III in urine
questions.concept: Urinary loss of antithrombin III together with increased hepatic synthesis of fibrinogen creates a hypercoagulable state; renal vein thrombosis is the classical complication and is commonest in membranous nephropathy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The treatment of choice for a 4-year-old child with typical steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome is:
questions.concept: Oral prednisolone is first line in childhood nephrotic syndrome, and biopsy is reserved for atypical features such as age below 1 year, haematuria, hypertension, renal failure or steroid resistance.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Tubulointerstitial disease, RTA & renal replacement therapy
questions.stem: Type 1 (distal) renal tubular acidosis characteristically causes:
options: Hypokalaemia with nephrolithiasis and inability to acidify urine
questions.concept: Distal RTA reflects failure of hydrogen ion secretion in the collecting duct, giving hyperchloraemic normal anion gap acidosis with inappropriately alkaline urine, hypokalaemia, hypercalciuria and calcium phosphate stones.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Tubulointerstitial Diseases of the Kidney

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Tubulointerstitial disease, RTA & renal replacement therapy
questions.stem: Fanconi syndrome comprises:
options: Proximal tubular loss of glucose, amino acids, phosphate and bicarbonate
questions.concept: Fanconi syndrome is generalised proximal tubular dysfunction causing glycosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, uricosuria and type 2 RTA, with rickets or osteomalacia; causes include cystinosis, Wilson disease, myeloma and tenofovir.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Tubulointerstitial Diseases of the Kidney

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Tubulointerstitial disease, RTA & renal replacement therapy
questions.stem: Type 4 renal tubular acidosis is distinguished from types 1 and 2 by the presence of:
questions.concept: Type 4 RTA results from aldosterone deficiency or resistance and is the only type with hyperkalaemia; it is commonly seen in diabetic nephropathy and with ACE inhibitors or potassium-sparing diuretics.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Tubulointerstitial Diseases of the Kidney

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Tubulointerstitial disease, RTA & renal replacement therapy
questions.stem: Analgesic nephropathy is most classically associated with:
questions.concept: Chronic combined analgesic abuse, particularly phenacetin-containing compounds, causes chronic interstitial nephritis with renal papillary necrosis, sterile pyuria and a raised risk of urothelial carcinoma.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Tubulointerstitial Diseases of the Kidney

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Tubulointerstitial disease, RTA & renal replacement therapy
questions.stem: Acute interstitial nephritis due to a drug typically presents with:
options: Fever, rash, eosinophilia and white cell casts with acute kidney injury
questions.concept: Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis, classically from penicillins, NSAIDs, rifampicin or proton pump inhibitors, gives fever, rash, peripheral eosinophilia, eosinophiluria and sterile pyuria with white cell casts. Withdrawal of the drug is the mainstay.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Tubulointerstitial Diseases of the Kidney

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Tubulointerstitial disease, RTA & renal replacement therapy
questions.stem: In distal renal tubular acidosis the urinary anion gap is:
options: Negative because of high ammonium excretion
Positive because of impaired ammonium excretion
questions.concept: A positive urinary anion gap (sodium plus potassium minus chloride) indicates low urinary ammonium and therefore a renal cause of normal anion gap acidosis, whereas diarrhoeal bicarbonate loss gives a negative gap with appropriately high ammonium.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Tubulointerstitial Diseases of the Kidney

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Tubulointerstitial disease, RTA & renal replacement therapy
questions.stem: The commonest indication for initiating maintenance dialysis in chronic kidney disease is:
options: Refractory uraemic symptoms with volume overload or hyperkalaemia
questions.concept: Dialysis is started for uraemic symptoms, refractory fluid overload, hyperkalaemia, acidosis or pericarditis rather than for a fixed level of glomerular filtration rate; anaemia and bone disease are managed medically.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Tubulointerstitial Diseases of the Kidney

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Tubulointerstitial disease, RTA & renal replacement therapy
questions.stem: Which is an absolute contraindication to peritoneal dialysis?
options: Documented loss of peritoneal membrane function or extensive adhesions
questions.concept: Loss of peritoneal function or extensive intra-abdominal adhesions preclude peritoneal dialysis. Diabetes is in fact often well suited to it, and previous surgery is only a relative concern.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Tubulointerstitial Diseases of the Kidney

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Tubulointerstitial disease, RTA & renal replacement therapy
questions.stem: Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome is caused by:
options: Rapid urea removal creating a cerebral osmotic gradient and cerebral oedema
questions.concept: Rapid clearance of urea from blood leaves brain urea relatively high, drawing water into the brain and causing headache, nausea, confusion and seizures. It is prevented by short, slow initial sessions in patients with very high urea.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Tubulointerstitial Diseases of the Kidney

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Tubulointerstitial disease, RTA & renal replacement therapy
questions.stem: The best long-term renal replacement option for a young patient with end-stage renal disease is:
questions.concept: Renal transplantation gives the best survival and quality of life in suitable candidates, with living related donation offering superior graft survival. Dialysis is a bridge to transplantation.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Tubulointerstitial Diseases of the Kidney

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The commonest cause of peripheral neuropathy worldwide is:
questions.concept: Diabetes mellitus is the commonest cause of peripheral neuropathy, typically a symmetrical distal sensory polyneuropathy in a glove-and-stocking distribution. Leprosy remains the commonest cause of treatable neuropathy in endemic regions.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Guillain-Barre syndrome most characteristically presents with:
options: Descending flaccid paralysis with early sphincter involvement
Ascending symmetrical flaccid paralysis with areflexia and preserved sphincters
Spastic paraparesis with a sensory level
Proximal weakness with a heliotrope rash
questions.concept: Guillain-Barre syndrome is an acute ascending symmetrical flaccid areflexic paralysis, often after Campylobacter jejuni infection, with sparing of sphincters and relatively minor sensory signs. Respiratory failure is the main danger.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The characteristic cerebrospinal fluid finding in Guillain-Barre syndrome is:
options: Raised protein with normal cell count (albuminocytological dissociation)
questions.concept: Albuminocytological dissociation - raised protein with a normal cell count - is characteristic, though it may be absent in the first week. More than 50 cells per microlitre should prompt a search for HIV or other causes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The treatment of choice for Guillain-Barre syndrome with rapidly progressive weakness is:
questions.concept: Intravenous immunoglobulin and plasma exchange are equally effective and are the mainstay; corticosteroids are ineffective and are not recommended. Serial vital capacity monitoring guides the need for ventilation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Myasthenia gravis is caused by antibodies most commonly directed against:
questions.concept: About 85% of generalised myasthenia gravis patients have antibodies to the postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptor; most of the remainder have anti-MuSK antibodies. Weakness worsens with repeated activity and improves with rest.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome from myasthenia gravis?
options: Improvement of power with sustained or repeated exercise
questions.concept: In Lambert-Eaton syndrome, antibodies to presynaptic P/Q-type calcium channels reduce acetylcholine release, and power improves with brief exercise (post-tetanic potentiation), with an incremental response on high-frequency repetitive stimulation. It is often paraneoplastic with small cell lung cancer.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The investigation of choice to confirm neuromuscular junction dysfunction in myasthenia gravis is:
options: Repetitive nerve stimulation showing a decremental response
questions.concept: Low-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation shows a decremental response of more than 10%, and single-fibre EMG is the most sensitive electrophysiological test. Creatine kinase is normal, unlike in myopathy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: All patients with newly diagnosed myasthenia gravis should undergo:
options: Computed tomography of the chest for thymoma
questions.concept: About 10 to 15% of myasthenia patients have a thymoma and up to 65% thymic hyperplasia, so chest imaging is mandatory; thymectomy benefits patients with thymoma and many generalised seronegative-for-MuSK cases.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Which drug should be avoided in a patient with myasthenia gravis?
questions.concept: Aminoglycosides, along with quinine, quinolones, magnesium, beta blockers and neuromuscular blockers, impair neuromuscular transmission and can precipitate a myasthenic crisis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with leprosy has a thickened ulnar nerve with claw hand. The nerve is most commonly involved at the:
options: Elbow, just above the medial epicondyle
questions.concept: In leprosy the ulnar nerve is the most frequently affected nerve and is thickened and tender about 2 to 5 cm proximal to the medial epicondyle, where it is superficial and cooler - bacilli favour cooler sites.
